source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Because we want to move as quickly as possible, could we target late TUESDAY for delivery? Please begin the model build using the information currently available, and we can refine it as further inputs are confirmed.

The present data position is as follows:

1) The attached CargoNest feasibility/demand analysis, TransitGrid-Market-Forecast, may be used directionally together with the assumptions in the brief.

2) Capex figures have not yet been finalized. The overall program is presently estimated at 225–270M, so please use the midpoint of the ranges in the brief. The attached business case also shows the midpoint set.

3) Firm figures for land values, lease costs, opex, and pricing are not yet available. Use the indicative ranges in the document and clearly flag every resulting assumption.

4) Financing terms remain unconfirmed, with no lender or investor commitments at this stage. Please apply standard market assumptions selected from the ranges provided.

5) Structured site-level information, including traffic counts and land status, is not yet available. We only have a general traffic count for each corridor, so the missing site-level details must be modeled.

6) Use AUD and a 2031 base year for the model.

7) The core requirement is to model correctly and clearly demonstrate why availability-style payments are necessary to make the project viable and bankable. This is the primary information the government wants to see.

Accordingly, treat the brief and attached materials as the main reference points, annotate all assumptions clearly, and proceed now. We will iterate when more definitive inputs become available. Please let me know if anything critical arises during the build.

source_message.speaker: freelancer
source_message.text:
Hi Mari,

Sure I will make the required changes. The model looks detailed because it's built on individual drivers each revenue stream (parking, pods, fleet, digital, ancillary) and each cost line is calculated separately from its own assumption, rather than typed in as one lump number. I did it this way on purpose so that when the government reviewer asks "where does this figure come from?", every number traces back to a source on the Assumptions tab. That's what makes it defensible.

The trade-off is exactly what you're feeling , more drivers , more rows to look at. I can go either way, so I'd rather you decide:

(a) Keep it driver-based (defensible, more rows), or
(b) Collapse it to a summary model a handful of top-level lines (total revenue, total cost, debt, availability payment, returns) with the detailed build moved to hidden/backing tabs. The front page becomes very short and clean; the detail is still there if anyone wants to open it.

I can make it a one-pager but still has the audit trail underneath. Tell me which you'd prefer and I'll restructure accordingly.

A few structuring options came up that could genuinely strengthen your pitch to government. These aren't in the model yet; I'm flagging them because any one of them could be the thing that makes the submission stand out. Such as:

1\. Government-funds-first, then sublet against the income ("build-then-transfer"). The Province funds or co-funds the capex up front (cheapest capital in the room), then leases/sublets the operating network to a private operator who pays a concession fee back against parking, pod and fleet income. This flips the story instead of government paying an availability payment out, government recovers a return in. I can model this as a third case (Case H) it may show a far lower net cost to the Province than the availability-payment route.

2\. Availability payment now, tapering to a revenue-share later. Rather than a flat 24-year payment, structure it so the Province pays more in the early ramp-up years (when revenue is thin) and then, once the network matures and throws off surplus cash, the Province shares in the upside clawing back part of what it paid in. Same bankability, lower lifetime net cost, and it reads as a partnership rather than a subsidy.

3\. Toll / user-levy overlay on the corridor. If these sites sit on designated freight corridors, a small per-truck corridor levy (or a portion of an existing road-use charge) could be ring-fenced to part-fund the network. That directly reduces the availability payment the government has to find from general revenue the users who benefit help pay.

4\. Phased equity exit / refinancing at stabilisation. Model the Province (or the original equity) selling down its stake to a pension fund or infrastructure fund once the network is built and de-risked (around year 9-12). De-risked, cash-yielding infrastructure sells at a premium so early capital gets recycled out at a profit and redeployed into Phase 4, instead of being locked up for 24 years.

5\. Anchor / cornerstone tenant revenue. Lock in four or five large fleets or a fuel/EV/retail partner on a long-term take-or-pay contract at the flagship hubs before financial close. Even a modest guaranteed floor on revenue materially improves the DSCR and can shrink the availability payment lenders require it's the single fastest way to make the numbers look stronger without changing the build.

Happy to build any of these into the model as additional cases options 1 and 2 in particular could meaningfully cut the headline cost to government, which is exactly what makes a submission persuasive. Let me know which direction you'd like, and whether to go simple (b) or keep it detailed, and I'll turn it around.

Best,
Elias

execution.observed_behavior: Freelancer reports that parking, pods, fleet, digital, and ancillary revenue streams were built separately from individual drivers rather than entered as one lump-sum revenue figure.
